The Fight · Saturday, November 14, 2026 · 8:00 PM ET / 5:00 PM PT · DAZN, TNT and truTV · Main-event ring walk about 11:10 PM ET
The Read — Main Event
⚑ Blotter Flag · Narrative Spine
Darius Fulghum has been past round eight twice against real opposition, and both times the fight turned on him late: dropped in the 12th by Bektemir Melikuziev, staggered by a jab in the 8th by David Stevens. Diego Pacheco's best work comes after eight. He got up off the floor against Kevin Lele Sadjo and closed the fight, and he broke Immanuwel Aleem down in the 11th in this building in July. The first half belongs to whoever owns the inside. The second half is the fight.
The Fight Lives After Eight
Pacheco brings the size, the home crowd and the 12-round miles. Fulghum brings what Pacheco's last four opponents didn't: a habit of turning clean fights into close, ugly ones. How long he can keep it ugly decides the night.

Pacheco is 26-0 with 19 knockouts, a 25-year-old from Los Angeles fighting for the second straight time in a building where he has already stopped two men. 2025 was his long year. He went 12 rounds three times, against Steven Nelson in January, Trevor McCumby in July and Kevin Lele Sadjo in December. Sadjo put him down in the eighth, the first knockdown of his career. He got up and finished with his three busiest rounds of the night, and had Sadjo in trouble at the end. Then he changed corners, bringing in Buddy McGirt, and in July he walked down Immanuwel Aleem for ten rounds before dropping and stopping him in the eleventh. He comes in ranked first by the WBC and second by the WBO. "As a fighter trying to get to the top, I'm over here sometimes doing too much," he said, talking about his work with McGirt.

Fulghum took the long road. He turned pro at 25 after earning a nursing degree at Prairie View A&M, stopped his first eight men, and got his real test in May 2025: a WBA eliminator with Bektemir Melikuziev in Las Vegas. It was level going into the last round and close on the punch count all night. Then a left to the body and one upstairs put him down in the 12th, and he lost 114-112 on all three cards. Six months later he fought David Stevens to a majority draw in ten rounds of holding and wrestling, and got staggered by a jab late in the eighth. In May he got back on track, a body shot that made Urrutia's corner quit after three. "The winner of this fight puts us at the door of a world title opportunity," he said.

The size is all one way. Pacheco is three inches taller, weighed in at 168 to Fulghum's 167.7, and works behind a long jab that sets up the body. Fulghum wants to be inside, where he can bang the body and lean. He outworked Melikuziev downstairs in the middle rounds, but his fights at distance have a way of turning into clinches. Alantez Fox tied him up for ten rounds and one judge scored it even, and the Stevens fight went the same way.

The first four rounds are Fulghum's window. He is quick, he punches in short bunches, and Pacheco has shown he can be hit; Sadjo found him. If Fulghum can hold Pacheco up, win the exchanges on the inside and keep it a hugging fight, he can steal rounds and make the cards close. But after eight, the history points one way. Pacheco's output went up late against Sadjo and Aleem, and Fulghum's legs have been tested late twice and found short both times. Watch his feet in the ninth.

Championship Round Bank
Diego Pacheco
Deep
Sixteen rounds at nine or later: the full 12 against Nelson, McCumby and Sadjo, into the 11th against Aleem and the 9th against Coceres. He went down in Sadjo's fight and still finished it on top.
Darius Fulghum
Moderate
One 12-rounder, against a ranked contender in Melikuziev, plus three 10-rounders (Fox, Alexander, Stevens). The one time he reached the 12th, he was dropped in it.
Crisis Execution Rating
Diego Pacheco
Tier I
Down for the first time in his career in round eight against Sadjo, he answered with his three busiest rounds, 10 through 12, and had Sadjo in trouble at the end. Output went up when the fight got hard.
Darius Fulghum
Tier II
Hurt in the third by Melikuziev, he came back strong through the middle rounds on body work. Dropped in the 12th, he got up and finished on his feet. He doesn't fold. The question is whether his plan holds when he's tired.
Judge's Chair
How This Gets Scored
Decision Risk: Medium

Judges reward clean punches first, then effective aggression. Pacheco's jab and straight right land clean from range and look like scoring shots from ringside. Fulghum's best work is short body shots inside, which land but are harder to see, and holding wipes out a round's work for both men. His last two fights past six rounds both ended close: 114-112 against him on every card, then a majority draw.

This is Pacheco's city and his second straight fight in this building. In a round with no clear winner, the crowd noise usually goes his way.

Score it yourself: if Fulghum is winning the exchanges inside but the referee is breaking them every ten seconds, give Pacheco the rounds where his jab landed clean. That is how judges usually break a hugging round.
📋 Amateur Thread — Two Different Clocks
Pacheco started boxing at ten and finished his amateur career with more than 75 bouts and eight national championships across the United States and Mexico. Fulghum turned pro at 25 after college. Pacheco has been a professional for seven years; Fulghum, for four.
Pacheco wins if
  • The jab lands first and keeps Fulghum on the end of it through the opening four rounds.
  • He goes to the body early and doesn't let Fulghum be the only one working down there.
  • His output holds or rises after round eight, as it did against Sadjo and Aleem.
  • He punches out of the clinches instead of waiting for the break.
Fulghum wins if
  • He gets inside in the first two rounds and makes Pacheco fight at his range.
  • He lands enough to the body to slow Pacheco's legs before the second half.
  • The clinches stay long enough to take Pacheco's rhythm, and short enough that the referee doesn't take a point.
  • He is still moving his feet in round nine.
Blotter Call · Main Event · Lean
Diego Pacheco — Stoppage
Pacheco's two stoppages in this building came in the sixth (Sulecki) and the eleventh (Aleem), and his output rises after eight. Fulghum has never been stopped, but both of his long fights cracked late. It's a Lean because he has only 17 fights and keeps getting up. The upset is a clinch-heavy, ugly 12 rounds that the judges can't separate.

How to Read the Blotter Mark

Each Call sits on a nine-slot line. Our pick is always on the left; his opponent is on the right; the middle slot is a draw. The shaded slot is our mark: the one result we are calling. After the fight, the recap puts a second marker where the ring actually landed and counts the steps between the two. The closer the marks, the better the Call.

Yuberjen Martinez
Co-Main · Flyweight · 12 Rounds · Main Card
Olascuaga vs. Martinez
Olascuaga's WBO flyweight title
Anthony Olascuaga
12-1 · 9 KOs · Los Angeles
Orthodox · 27 · WBO champion · Stopped his last three: Iimura (R9), Kuwahara (R4), Camacho-Rivera (R2)
vs
Yuberjen Martinez
7-0 · 7 KOs · Turbo, Colombia
Orthodox · 35 · 2016 Olympic silver (light flyweight) · 2017 World bronze · Turned pro at 30
Martinez won Colombia's first Olympic boxing medal in 28 years in Rio, losing the final to Hasanboy Dusmatov, and has knocked out all seven men he has fought as a pro, most recently Angel Bethancourt in May. But he is 35 and has seven pro fights; Olascuaga has 13 and has already been to the hard places. He was stopped in nine by Kenshiro Teraji in 2023, went 12 to beat Hiroto Kyoguchi in 2025, and has stopped his last three opponents. The amateur pedigree says Martinez won't be outclassed early. The champion's pro rounds say he wins the second half.
Blotter Call · Co-Main · Lean Anthony Olascuaga — UD Olascuaga's recent run is all stoppages, but Martinez has never been stopped and has no history of fading that would justify calling one. The edge is 12-round experience, so the Call is the cards.

The Blotter Spotlight — Pacheco
Federico Pacheco Jr.
⚡ Scout's Chair — The Fighter You Need to Know
Federico Pacheco Jr.
11-0 · 8 KOs · Heavyweight · Diego's younger brother

We found Federico through his brother's story, and he has been worth following on his own. His amateur run was short by heavyweight standards: Youth Nationals, then a pro start at 19 in late 2022. Most of his education came in Southern California sparring rooms with Zhilei Zhang, Frank Sanchez and Arslanbek Makhmudov. In July, on Diego's card in this building, he stopped Nick Jones in the second round.

He hasn't always looked finished. A messy six-round decision over Calvin Barnett last year showed how much he was still learning. Tonight's opponent, Jack May, is 11-1 with 10 knockouts, the kind of puncher who makes a young heavyweight keep his hands up for eight rounds. If Federico handles him, the conversation about him starts to be about him, not his last name.

Fighter Environment
Environment Analysis · Dignity Health Sports Park
Diego Pacheco: Home city, home promoter, second straight fight in this building, and second fight with McGirt. A win keeps him in line for a title shot.

Darius Fulghum: A Golden Boy fighter on a Matchroom show, the B-side in the A-side's market. He trains with Darnell Pierce and calls it the fight that opens the door to a title shot. The crowd will be loud for the other corner.
Rules Referenced
Rule 29 — Durability: a stoppage Call needs a finisher and a documented weakness on the other side. Martinez has none on record, so Olascuaga's Call is a decision. Rule 46 — Fighter Environment: trainer, promoter, crowd and setting. Rule 81 — Championship Round Bank, Crisis Execution Rating and Judge's Chair run in every issue. Rule 86 — Details from secondary sources are labeled as such. Rule 90 — Knockouts beside every record. Rules 95 and 105 — Calls go on the broadcast card only, and the card is laid out the way it airs. Rule 111 — Every Call is labeled High or Lean. Rule 112 — How Each Fighter Wins. Rule 113 — Blotter Mark and Proofline: the shaded slot is our Call; the recap adds the result. Rule 115 — Every Blotter Call is one winner and one way the fight ends. We never hedge between outcomes, and a draw is a legitimate prediction.

Rule 114 · Also Today — When more than one card runs on the same date, one card is featured and gets the full program and every Call. Carson is featured tonight because it carries the world title fight and two fighters from our Grind and Climb list. Riyadh gets a compact section: matchup, records with knockouts, start time and one scouting note, with no Calls.

Watch For
Fulghum's feet in round nine
Both of his long fights cracked late. If he's still moving at nine, the fight is live.
The referee and the clinch
Long clinches help Fulghum. Quick breaks help Pacheco's jab.
Who works the body first
Fulghum wants to own it. If Pacheco gets there first, Fulghum's best weapon is gone.
Martinez after six
He has never needed the second half as a pro. Tonight he might.
